sentences.text: Eudimorphodon was a small pterosaur with a wingspan of roughly 100 centimeters and a total body length of about one meter.
Its anatomy featured a very large fourth finger that supported the wing membrane.
The skull contained sharp fangs followed by smaller, multi-cusped teeth designed for processing food.
This specific arrangement of multi-cusped teeth distinguishes the animal from almost all other pterosaurs, which typically possessed simple teeth or none at all.
Eudimorphodon possessed the strongest dental occlusion known among pterosaurs, allowing its top and bottom teeth to touch directly when the jaws closed.
Evidence of tooth wear suggests the animal could crush or chew its food rather than just swallowing it whole.
The genus was discovered in 1973 by Mario Pandolfi in Cene, Italy, and described by Rocco Zambelli the same year.
Fossil jaw fragments bearing multi-cusped teeth were later found in 1986 in the Dockum Group rocks of western Texas.
There are currently 13 recorded fossil occurrences of this genus.
Stomach contents preserved in fossils confirm that Eudimorphodon was piscivorous, having consumed fish of the genus Parapholidophorus.
Wear patterns along the sides of its teeth indicate the animal likely fed on hard-shelled invertebrates as well.

Eudimorphodon is believed to be a member of the specialized off-branch Campylognathoididae, though a 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron suggests it groups with the clade Novialoidea within Lonchognatha, differing from this placement.
Eudimorphodon lived during the Late Triassic, spanning from 219 to 215 million years ago.
